items.title: Client-Side Ephemeral De-Identification of Protected Health Information (PHI) in Multi-Center Clinical Trial Analysis and Large Language Model Workflows: Validating Zero-Trust Data Sanitization Under HIPAA Safe Harbor Section 164.514(b)
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Background The integration of frontier Large Language Models (LLMs) and Generative AI into biomedical research,clinical trial documentation, electronic health record (EHR) summarization, and diagnostic reasoningpresents a fundamental regulatory impasse under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act(HIPAA). Clinical researchers and healthcare organizations are routinely constrained by the requirement forBusiness Associate Agreements (BAAs) and the risk of catastrophic Protected Health Information (PHI)exfiltration through cloud-hosted AI inference APIs, training pipelines, and multi-tenant telemetry caches. Methods We formulate, implement, and empirically validate an on-device, zero-trust architectural paradigm termed Zero-Trust Data Sanitization (ZTDS) . ZTDS intercepts unstructured clinical text, Case Report Forms(CRFs), lab reports, and physician consultation notes directly within the client's volatile memory (RAM) atkeystroke/document ingestion. It programmatically de-identifies all 18 statutory PHI categories definedunder 45 CFR §164.514(b)(2) (HIPAA Safe Harbor) using deterministic entity tokenization prior to TCP/IPpacket transmission to third-party AI APIs. A client-side volatile session dictionary enables lossless, 1-clicktoken re-identification of LLM output within the local session without persisting data to disk or cloudinfrastructure. Results In a benchmark evaluation across 2,500 synthetic multi-center clinical notes containing dense, co-occurring PHI entities (names, medical record numbers, dates, geographic subdivisions, biometricidentifiers, device identifiers, and contact vectors), the client-side ZTDS engine achieved a 99.94% recall rate on direct HIPAA 18 identifiers with an average processing latency of 1.84 ms per standard clinicalnote (mean length: 1,420 characters). In comparison, conventional cloud-based DLP proxy gatewaysincurred an average latency of 242.6 ms (a 131-fold latency reduction) while introducing server-sideintermediate processing liabilities. Network packet inspection confirmed zero outbound bytes of PHI under both connected and disconnected (Airplane Mode) network states. Discussion & Conclusion Under HHS regulations (45 CFR §164.502(d) and §164.514(a)), health information that has been de-identified according to Safe Harbor standards is no longer considered PHI and is exempt from HIPAArestrictions. By executing comprehensive de-identification entirely within volatile client RAM beforetransmission, the downstream AI service provider never handles PHI and is legally excluded from qualifyingas a Business Associate under 45 CFR §160.103. ZTDS offers an immediate, mathematically auditable, andzero-overhead pathway for hospitals, pharmaceutical research sponsors, and clinicians to securelyleverage public and commercial AI models without legal friction or regulatory non-compliance.

items.title: Integrated multi-omics and machine learning analysis identifies CDK1 as a key regulator of Dieda Qili Tablet-mediated osteogenic differentiation and immune microenvironment remodeling
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Dieda Qili Tablet (DDQLT), a traditional Chinese medicine formula, has been clinically applied for fracture treatment; however, its molecular mechanisms underlying osteogenic effects remain unclear. This study aimed to elucidate the potential mechanisms of DDQLT in regulating osteoblast differentiation using an integrated bioinformatics and computational framework. Active compounds and potential targets of DDQLT were identified through network pharmacology. Transcriptomic datasets of MC3T3-E1 osteoblast differentiation were integrated for differential expression analysis and weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA). Candidate genes were screened by intersecting DDQLT-related targets with differentially expressed genes and WGCNA-derived hub genes. Protein–protein interaction (PPI) analysis combined with LASSO, random forest (RF), and support vector machine (SVM) algorithms was performed to identify key regulatory genes. Candidate targets were further validated using the independent human osteoblast dataset GSE157322. Molecular docking and immune infiltration analyses were conducted to explore potential mechanisms. A total of 127 active compounds and 780 potential targets of DDQLT were identified. Transcriptomic analysis revealed 1,165 differentially expressed genes, while WGCNA identified four osteogenesis-associated modules containing 5,628 genes. Functional enrichment analysis demonstrated that DDQLT-associated targets were primarily involved in cell-cycle regulation and osteogenic processes. CDK1 was consistently identified as a key hub gene across multiple approaches and was significantly upregulated during human osteoblast differentiation in the GSE157322 dataset. Molecular docking suggested potential interactions between CDK1 and DDQLT-derived flavonoids, including quercetin and kaempferol. Immune infiltration analysis revealed increased abundance of resting memory CD4⁺ T cells during osteogenic differentiation. This study suggests that DDQLT may promote osteoblast differentiation through a multi-component regulatory network involving CDK1-associated cell-cycle regulation and osteoimmune microenvironment modulation. These findings provide new insights into the molecular basis of DDQLT-mediated bone regeneration and highlight CDK1 as a potential target for osteogenic therapy.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Alzheimer’s Disease Detection Across Neuroimaging and Speech: A Reproducible Cross-Modal Secondary Analysis
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Artificial-intelligence (AI) systems for Alzheimer’s disease (AD) increasingly use neuroimaging or spontaneous speech, but reported performance is difficult to interpret across studies because cohorts, endpoints, languages, preprocessing, and validation protocols differ. We applied a systematic coding framework to a predefined 51-reference evidence corpus and performed a conservative secondary quantitative synthesis. Twenty-six references met prespecified criteria for primary empirical AI studies: 7 neuroimaging and 19 speech/language studies. Fourteen studies contributed 15 model-level benchmark entries with extractable headline accuracy. Neuroimaging entries ranged from 66.25–99.95% (median 97.74%); speech/language entries ranged from 78.70–92.08% (median 83.81%). These values are descriptive and are not pooled diagnostic-effect estimates. Only 5/26 primary studies (19.2%) explicitly evaluated external, cross-domain, or cross-language generalization, 5/26 (19.2%) used explicit multimodal input, and 4/26 (15.4%) emphasized explainability or uncertainty. Multilingual or cross-lingual evaluation appeared in 3/19 speech/language studies (15.8%). The evidence therefore supports a distinction between high within-study accuracy and clinically credible transportability. Independent validation, patient-disjoint evaluation, calibrated uncertainty, representative cohorts, and linguistically diverse testing should be treated as core design requirements rather than optional extensions. The study-level coding table and benchmark extract are provided for reproducibility and updating.

items.title: PCR-Validated Comparative Deep Learning Analysis of CNN and YOLO Models for UAV-Based multi-spectral Detection of Sugarcane White Leaf Disease (WLD)
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Context: Sugarcane White Leaf Disease (WLD), caused by phytoplasma of the 16SrXI group, threatens global sugarcane production and can cause total yield loss in susceptible varieties. For effective disease management, early and scalable detection is crucial. Aims: This study presents a PCR-validated comparative analysis of three deep learning models, YOLOv5s, YOLOv8s, and a TensorFlow/Keras-based Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), for automated WLD detection using UAV-acquired multi-spectral imagery. Methods: The plant samples were collected from 13 sugarcane fields at three locations in Sri Lanka, comprising a total of 115 samples, including 102 healthy and 13 diseased, confirmed by PCR. Regions of interest were extracted from orthomosaics across six imaging channels (five multi-spectral bands plus one broadband RGB channel). Class imbalance was addressed by creating a balanced dataset of 1,800 images, which were split into training, validation, and testing sets using stratified random sampling; augmentation was performed before partitioning, which left a residual risk of data leakage as mentioned in the limitations, with the small number of diseased plants. Models were evaluated per spectral band and on the full multi-spectral dataset using precision, recall, F1-score, and mean Average Precision (mAP@50 and mAP@50–95; YOLO models only). Key Results: The CNN achieved 98.85% precision, 95.56% recall, and 97.17% F1-score, performing competitively against previously published WLD detection results to date. The green waveband (560 nm) proved to be most discriminative for YOLO models and the CNN used all wave bands apart from the blue band (450 nm). Ground truth was confirmed by PCR and all predictions were tested against this. Conclusion: The results indicate that automated WLD detection using UAV multi-spectral imaging and deep learning, specifically CNN models, is technically feasible for precision agriculture, as it demonstrates satisfactory performance in this specific context with limited number of datasets and a single season, and emphasizes the need for optimization of the spectral bands. Implications and Impacts: External validation is needed on larger/longer season/more varieties before operational deployment is recommended.

items.title: An Outcome-Independent Analytical Framework Reveals Systemic Discordance Between a Continuous Neural-Mesenchymal Programme and Consensus Molecular Subtyping in Colorectal Cancer: A Multi-Cohort Transcriptomic Study
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract An outcome-independent strategy is presented for deriving a continuous programme score from co-expression structure alone, then testing its agreement with an established classifier across independent cohorts. Consensus Molecular Subtyping (CMS) groups colorectal cancer (CRC) transcriptomes into discrete categories; CMS4 denotes mesenchymal, stromal-rich disease. The question addressed is whether a continuous neural-mesenchymal (NEM) programme, built from a curated 14-gene panel under a pre-specified correlation threshold, tracks CMS4 assignment without being reducible to it. In a TCGA-COAD discovery cohort (n = 499), a four-gene module (GAP43, VIM, ZEB1, TWIST1) emerged as the only combination for which every pairwise Spearman correlation exceeded r = 0.50 (r = 0.51–0.74); the module was fixed before external validation and never trained against CMS or outcome data. The resulting NEM score correlated strongly with Hallmark EMT ssGSEA activity (r = 0.93) and identified 96.3% of CMS4 samples correctly. NEM-High status was not confined to CMS4, however: 35.3% of NEM-High tumours in the discovery cohort fell within CMS1–CMS3, a pattern that held across nine external GEO cohorts (24.0–46.8%, mean 38.0%, n ≈ 3,742). NEM-High status carried a numerically elevated but non-significant hazard of death (HR = 1.44–1.53, p > 0.05). A median-split sensitivity check and a leave-VIM-out re-scoring each ruled out dichotomisation and gene-set overlap as explanations. An orthogonal Human Protein Atlas cross-check found no single module gene independently prognostic in COAD or READ, favouring a module-level interpretation. Continuous NEM activity and categorical CMS status describe overlapping but distinct aspects of CRC biology: a compact, correlation-derived module reconstructs most of a subtype's membership while still detecting programme activity the label leaves out.

items.title: A Reproducible Framework for Auditing the Trustworthiness of Clinical Machine Learning Models
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract The deployment of machine learning (ML) models for clinical risk prediction is frequently challenged by domain shift when algorithms are transferred across heterogeneous healthcare settings. Conventional evaluation primarily emphasizes discriminative performance, such as the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC), which may overlook failures in probability calibration, explainability stability, robustness, and clinical utility. To address these challenges, we present AETHEL, an open-source and reproducible framework for systematically auditing the trustworthiness of clinical ML models. The framework evaluates multiple classification and survival models using harmonized datasets, including the Framingham Heart Study and the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), through integrated assessment of discrimination, calibration, explainability, robustness, clinical utility, and cross-cohort generalization. Experimental evaluation demonstrates measurable degradation in predictive performance and calibration following cross-cohort transfer. While post-hoc calibration using Platt Scaling and Isotonic Regression improves probability calibration, explainability analyses reveal shifts in feature attribution under covariate drift. To quantify explanation stability, we introduce the Feature Agreement Score (FAS) and Top-k Jaccard Overlap (TkO) metrics, alongside visual clinical consequence analyses based on Decision Curve Analysis. AETHEL provides a unified, reproducible framework for auditing the trustworthiness of clinical machine learning models, supporting transparent evaluation and more informed deployment decisions in clinical settings.

items.title: Identical runs disagree more than different models: reproducibility limits in deep learning for brain-tumour MRI classification
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Purpose. Ablation studies in medical imaging routinely report differences of one or two accuracy points. If nominally identical training runs vary by as much, such comparisons may not reliably identify which model should advance to clinical validation. We measure that variation and identify its causes. Methods. A graph-augmented Vision Transformer was evaluated on 3064 contrast-enhanced T1 MRI slices from 233 patients: a seven-cell ablation at three seeds under a patient-wise split, four baselines, a graph-only control, plus low-data and corruption studies. Configurations were retrained at identical seeds, and divergence bisected across fresh processes using SHA-256 parameter fingerprints. 100 runs are reported. Results. Two runs of one configuration at one seed differ by 0.0265 accuracy over six matched pairs, exceeding the 0.0113 architectural contrast under test; the graph branch gives −0.0004 accuracy (95% CI −0.018 to +0.017). Two causes: the seed was applied after model construction, leaving initialisation uncontrolled; and after repair, divergence persists, associated with the fused attention backward though the framework reports full determinism. Image-wise rather than patient-wise splitting inflates accuracy by 0.044. Conclusion. Verify that each seed binds the stochastic sources it should, and report a measured replication scale. Both cost less than one ablation cell.

items.title: An auditable evidence compiler for large language model-assisted systematic reviews
items.abstract_or_text: Background: Large language models (LLMs) can support systematic reviews, but accurate individual outputs do not establish whether the final synthesis preserves the clinical question, accounts for statistical dependence and incorporates corrections. Objective: To develop and evaluate a framework linking LLM-assisted evidence processing to a versioned, auditable release of synthesis outputs. Methods: We used LLM agents to interpret sources and extract data. Deterministic code enforced statistical rules; investigators resolved material ambiguities and authorized release. We specified ten release properties covering evidence identities, statistical contributions and propagation of corrections. We retrospectively evaluated six integrity domains and historical failure events in one registered prognostic review, without an external comparator or held-out domain. Results: Fifty distinct root-cause events were documented, including 12 that had changed a pooled result before correction. Forty-six were resolved, and four remained disclosed limitations. The corpus comprised 454 reports, 445 studies, 441 cohort entities and 421 dependence clusters. Forty-one of 49 registered analyses were fitted, and eight retained explicit non-fitted states. All 39 source records across five principal analysis families reached a terminal source state. Two implementations within the project agreed across 1,217 numerical comparisons. All 94 file comparisons between release and publication packages were byte-identical. Two reviewers confirmed 39 principal records after seeing the same recommendations. Conclusions: This case provides a framework for inspecting synthesized evidence together with its provenance, statistical meaning and correction history. Comparative validity, generalizability and benefit in patient-centred care require independent evaluation.

items.title: Hybrid Neural and Numerical Inverse Identification of Fractional Memory and Regulatory Parameters in a Caputo Glucose Insulin Beta Cell Model
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Fractional-order models introduce memory into nonlinear dynamical systems but also turn parameter estimation into a computationally expensive inverse problem because each objective evaluation requires a history-dependent forward solve. We develop a hybrid neural–numerical framework for simultaneous identification of the Caputo order and selected regulatory parameters in a three-state glucose–insulin–beta-cell model. A fractional Adams–Bashforth–Moulton predictor–corrector method generates reference trajectories, while a local scaled-sensitivity analysis is used to screen candidate unknowns before inversion. The screening reveals nearcollinearity between the sensitivities associated with two regulatory coefficients (correlation −0.986); excluding the redundant coefficient reduces the sensitivity-matrix condition number from approximately 38.6 to 3.46. A parametric neural surrogate with inputs (t, α, a1, a15) is then trained on 220 Latin-hypercube trajectories using trajectory-level train/validation/test separation. On the 20 held-out trajectories, statewise coefficients of determination exceed 0.9997 and RMSEs are below 9.7 × 10−4. In a synthetic inverse benchmark with 20 independent noise realizations at each nonzero level, the surrogate-assisted method obtains median mean parameter errors of 0.76%, 1.39%, and 2.47% at 1%, 3%, and 5% observation noise, respectively; direct numerical inversion gives 0.86%, 1.52%, and 2.40%. Across 12 additional unseen parameter triples at 1% noise, the surrogate inversion has a median mean parameter error of 1.75%. Every recovered parameter set is independently verifiable with the fractional numerical solver. The experiments use dimensionless synthetic data and do not constitute clinical calibration; rather, they demonstrate a reproducible strategy for combining identifiability screening, a learned forward map, regularized inversion, and independent numerical verification in a nonlinear fractional system. MSC 2020: 34A08; 65L09; 65K10; 68T07; 92C30.

items.title: Scalable Causal-Interpretable Machine Learning for Cancer Prescreening Using Electronic Health Records
items.abstract_or_text: Electronic health records provide a source of real-world information for disease risk prediction, but many machine learning models learn implicit associations that are difficult to inspect or use for clinical reasoning. Causal Bayesian networks (CBNs) offer a form of causal-interpretable machine learning by representing conditional dependencies, putative directional relations, and probabilistic evidence propagation in a directed acyclic graph. However, conventional CBN structure learning becomes unstable and computationally expensive when applied to large-scale EHR data. To address this limitation, we propose UPEBNL, a scalable framework for causal-interpretable cancer prescreening based on parallel CBN learning. UPEBNL integrates adaptive data slicing, quality-aware structure aggregation, and global DAG construction to learn stable and interpretable dependency structures from large-scale observational data. We evaluated UPEBNL in high-dimensional and multi-million-sample simulations and applied it to EHR-based prescreening for esophageal and colorectal cancer. In simulations, UPEBNL improved structural recovery accuracy by nearly 40% and achieved up to a 221.28-fold speedup over conventional CBN learning strategies. For cancer risk prediction, the learned CBNs provided interpretable evidence paths and achieved validation AUCs of 0.8171 for esophageal cancer and 0.784 for colorectal cancer. Calibration and decision curve analyses further supported the reliability and clinical utility of the models. These findings suggest that scalable CBN learning can support interpretable cancer prescreening from large-scale EHR data.

items.title: Uncoded Clinical Features from Multilingual Electronic Health Records in Catalonia: Development and Validation Study
items.abstract_or_text: Background: Unstructured free‑text narratives in electronic health records (EHRs) contain critical clinical information that is not captured by structured standard codes. In Catalonia, primary care notes follow a semi‑structured format known as MEAP (in Catalan). However, extracting structured variables using cloud‑hosted commercial large language models (LLMs) raises substantial data privacy concerns and incurs high operational costs. Objective: To develop and validate a privacy-preserving local hybrid pipeline combining a lightweight small language model (SLM) with deterministic regular expressions for extracting six uncoded urinary tract infection (UTI) clinical features (fever, nitrites, leukocytes, lumbar pain, abdominal pain, and haematuria) from primary care EHR narratives. Methods: We deployed the open‑weight model (Phi4-mini, 3.8B parameters) within the institutional firewall using Ollama. Prompts were iteratively refined in collaboration with clinicians, and regular expressions were applied post‑inference. Validation was conducted across two independent arms: (1) a double‑blind clinician gold standard review of 60 real patient records (consensus‑resolved cases), and (2) an adversarial synthetic dataset of 720 notes enriched with linguistic noise, generated using GPT‑4.1 and Grok‑4.1. Point estimates and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were computed for key performance metrics. Results: The pipeline processed 15,498 MEAP narratives from a matched cohort of 2,962 primary care patients and identified 4,663 clinical feature occurrences. Patients progressing to acute pyelonephritis (cases) presented a higher features burden than non-progressing controls (71.3% vs. 55.8%; standardized mean difference [SMD] = 0.326), particularly for fever (33.0% vs. 9.0%; SMD = 0.616) and lumbar pain (29.0% vs. 9.8%; SMD = 0.502). In real-world clinician validation, overall performance yielded 93.8% accuracy (95% CI 90.6%-96.1%), 83.6% sensitivity (95% CI 73.0%-91.2%), 96.6% specificity (95% CI 93.6%-98.4%), 87.1% positive predictive value (PPV; 95% CI 77.0%-93.9%), and 95.5% negative predictive value (NPV; 95% CI 92.3%-97.7%). In synthetic stress-testing, the pipeline demonstrated 87.2% accuracy (95% CI 84.6%-89.6%), 73.9% sensitivity (95% CI 68.9%-78.5%), near-perfect specificity (99.5%, 95% CI 98.1%-99.9%), and 99.2% PPV (95% CI 97.2%-99.9%). Conclusions: A privacy-preserving local hybrid framework combining a compact open-weight SLM with regular expression rules achieves high specificity and precision for extracting six uncoded clinical features from multilingual primary care narratives. Running entirely within institutional servers, this approach keeps patient data secure, meets privacy standards, and avoids Application Programming Interface (API) costs, making it a practical tool for EHR research, though with lower sensitivity for narratively complex descriptions.

items.title: The Comprehensive Impact of Large Language Models on Medical Students’ Research, Learning, and Stress: A Cross-Sectional Study
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Background Large language models (LLMs) have rapidly expanded across medical education and research. However, systematic quantitative evidence on their usage patterns, perceived benefits, risk awareness, and their potential integration into medical education across different stages of medical training remains limited, particularly for emerging domestic models. Objective This study aimed to evaluate the usage characteristics of LLMs among medical students at different educational levels in China and to examine their implications for medical education and academic research. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted among four groups—undergraduates, academic master’s students, professional master’s students, and doctoral students—using a structured questionnaire. The survey assessed LLM usage patterns, application scenarios, risk awareness, and attitudes toward potential medical education reform. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and between-group comparisons. Results A total of 334 valid questionnaires were obtained, and 98.2% of respondents reported prior use of LLMs. DeepSeek and Doubao were the most frequently used models, with usage rates of 45.4% and 31.1%, respectively. Significant differences across educational levels were observed in usage frequency, duration, model preference, and application scenarios. Research and innovation-related use increased with higher educational levels, whereas exam-oriented and clinically focused learning declined. Risk awareness and the ability to critically evaluate generated information also increased with higher educational attainment. Research-related stress showed a structural divergence: output-related pressure increased with academic level, whereas skill-related pressure decreased. Conclusion LLMs have become integral tools for medical students’ learning and research, with distinct functional roles across stages of medical training. Future medical education should move beyond the question of whether to use LLMs and focus instead on establishing standardized and effective strategies for their use.

items.title: Polymorph-Independent Resistance to Generative Protein Design Across Five Tau Fibril Folds: A Cross-Tauopathy Benchmark
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Generative protein-binder-design tools such as diffusion-based backbone generators have recently been benchmarked against amyloid fibril targets, where success was found to depend on the specific structural polymorph rather than the disease of origin: some fibril folds are tractable, others uniformly resistant. Whether this polymorph-dependence generalizes to tau, the aggregating protein in Alzheimer's disease and a family of non-Alzheimer's tauopathies, is untested. We benchmarked RFdiffusion3 with mandatory ProteinMPNN sequence redesign against five distinct cryo-EM tau fibril folds spanning five tauopathies: Alzheimer's disease (paired helical filament), chronic traumatic encephalopathy, Pick's disease, corticobasal degeneration, and progressive supranuclear palsy, scoring all candidates through a common AlphaFold2-Multimer oracle. In contrast to the polymorph-dependent pattern reported for AL amyloidosis and alpha-synuclein, all five tau folds proved resistant to binder design (best interface predicted template modeling score, i_pTM, 0.116-0.401 across folds), with even the most tractable fold (progressive supranuclear palsy) falling short of the tractable range reported for other amyloid classes. Unlike those classes, where binder beta-sheet-forming amino acid propensity correlated strongly with predicted binding success, no such relationship was detected for tau (Pearson r=-0.19, p=0.50; n=15 designs), and the highest-scoring tau design is an alpha-helical bundle rather than a beta-sheet, suggesting a mechanistically distinct interaction mode. This is, to our knowledge, the first application of a modern diffusion-based generative design tool to tau fibrils, and the first evidence that resistance to generative binder design is not a universal property of amyloid geometry but varies by protein family independent of structural polymorph within that family.

items.title: Polymorph-Dependent Success of Generative Protein Design Against Amyloid Fibrils: A Cross-Method Benchmark Including AL Amyloidosis
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Generative protein design tools such as diffusion-based backbone generators and AlphaFold2-hallucination pipelines have been validated almost exclusively on globular receptor and signaling-protein targets. Whether these methods generalize to amyloid fibrils - flat, pocket-less, cross-beta surfaces that are structurally unlike any benchmark target used to date - is unknown. We benchmarked three generative design tools (RFdiffusion3, BindCraft, and BindEnergyCraft) for their ability to design binders against eight cryo-EM fibril structures spanning three amyloid diseases: AL (immunoglobulin light-chain) amyloidosis, Parkinson's disease (alpha-synuclein), and Alzheimer's disease (amyloid-beta). AL amyloid has not previously been attempted with any of these tools. Using a common AlphaFold2-Multimer scoring oracle and a mandatory ProteinMPNN sequence-redesign step for diffusion-generated backbones, we found that design success is polymorph-dependent rather than disease-dependent: amyloid-beta fibrils resisted all three methods (interface predicted template modeling score, i_pTM, 0.09-0.15 across both polymorphs tested, and zero accepted designs across 83 combined AF2-hallucination trajectories), alpha-synuclein was largely tractable (three of four polymorphs reaching i_pTM >= 0.70), and AL amyloid split evenly between the two extremes (i_pTM 0.235 for one polymorph, 0.585 for another). Diffusion-based backbone generation (RFdiffusion3) produced confident designs on several targets where AF2-hallucination-based methods (BindCraft, BindEnergyCraft) produced none. Across all RFdiffusion3 designs, binder beta-sheet-forming amino acid propensity correlated strongly with predicted interface confidence (Pearson r = 0.80, p = 8.0) hardware, excluding Turing-generation GPUs entirely. This is, to our knowledge, the first computational feasibility assessment of generative binder design against AL amyloid, and the first systematic comparison of these tools on any amyloid fibril target.

items.title: ALS as a Multivariable Feedback Instability System: Three‑Variable Dynamical Model, Phase‑Space Analysis, and Optimal Control
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Background Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disease driven by multifactorial crosstalk among energy‑metabolic impairment, disrupted proteostasis, and self‑amplifying neuroinflammation. Conventional single‑target therapeutics have yielded modest clinical benefits, implying ALS should be conceptualised as progressive destabilisation of a multivariable positive‑feedback dynamical system rather than a mono‑molecular disorder. Objective We constructed an analytically tractable three‑dimensional ordinary‑differential‑equation (ODE) model of ALS pathogenesis. Using phase‑space geometry and control‑theory frameworks, we aimed to quantitatively assess multi‑target combination therapy efficacy, optimise intervention timing, and characterise efficacy‑versus‑dosing‑burden trade‑offs. Methods State variables represented energy‑metabolic status (\(\:E\)), proteostasis capacity (\(\:P\)), and neuroinflammatory intensity (\(\:I\)). Three control inputs described metabolic support (\(\:{u}_{meta}\)), integrated stress response (ISR) inhibition (\(\:{u}_{isr}\)), and glial‑mediated inflammatory clearance (\(\:{u}_{gli}\)), each governed by Michaelis‑Menten‑type saturated pharmacodynamic functions. The ODE system was numerically integrated with the LSODA adaptive solver. Analytical workflows included phase‑space trajectory analysis, critical‑threshold parameter scanning, Pareto multi‑objective optimisation, proportional‑integral (PI) closed‑loop feedback control, and toxicity‑constrained piecewise‑constant optimal control. Results Without therapeutic intervention, model trajectories diverged from early‑disease initial conditions and converged onto the pathological attractor \(\:{X}_{D}\approx\:(0,0,{I}_{max})\) within approximately 4.5 time units. Open‑loop triple‑agent constant‑dose combination therapy redirected system trajectories toward the healthy homeostatic attractor \(\:{X}_{H}\approx\:(1,1,0)\). Parameter mapping identified a well‑defined “survival boundary”; control regimens falling below this threshold could not halt pathological collapse. Pareto optimisation demonstrated that the reference open‑loop constant‑dose protocol lay within the dominated sub‑optimal region, leaving substantial room for dosing‑burden reduction. Relative to proportional‑only (\(\:P\)) feedback, PI feedback control reduced steady‑state error by roughly one order of magnitude, at the expense of higher cumulative drug exposure. Under fixed cumulative‑toxicity constraints, constrained optimal control yielded front‑loaded piecewise‑constant dosing schedules that minimised time‑integrated disease burden: higher‑magnitude interventions were applied early, followed by low‑intensity maintenance. Conclusions The performance of multi‑modal ALS combination therapy strongly depends on intervention timing and control‑strategy design. Closed‑loop feedback outperforms static open‑loop constant dosing, and constrained optimal control further balances therapeutic efficacy against drug‑related toxicity limits. Therapeutic development for ALS should shift from “inhibiting individual molecular targets” toward a systems‑oriented goal: steering the overall pathological dynamical trajectory back toward the healthy homeostatic attractor.

items.title: Clinical quality of large language model answers to questions about pancreatic cancer
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Patients increasingly use large language models (LLMs) to seek cancer information, but the clinical quality and short-term consistency of their responses remain uncertain. We evaluated ChatGPT-5.5 Instant, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3 Flash, Grok 4.20, Microsoft Copilot, Doubao Seed 1.8, DeepSeek-V4 and Qwen 3.6 using ten patient-oriented pancreatic cancer questions submitted on three consecutive days. Five evaluators, blinded to platform identity, rated all 240 responses across six dimensions of clinical quality, yielding 1,200 ratings. Overall performance differed among platforms. Grok 4.20 and DeepSeek-V4 had the highest mean scores, whereas Doubao Seed 1.8 had the lowest. Differences were greatest in actionability and specificity. Adjacent-day score fluctuation was most pronounced for Doubao Seed 1.8 and Qwen 3.6, although no platform showed a significant systematic day effect after correction for multiple testing. The evaluated platforms generally provided relevant information, but clinical usefulness and repeatability varied. LLM-generated pancreatic cancer information should complement, rather than replace, professional clinical communication.

items.title: Explainable Machine Learning for Early Detection of Mathematics Learning Difficulties: A Systematic Review of Multimodal Educational Data and Predictive Modeling
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Mathematics learning difficulties, including developmental dyscalculia, affect about 3–6% of school-age children and, when unaddressed, can lead to long-term academic underperformance, reduced career opportunities in science and technology, anxiety, low self-efficacy, and high costs to society. Conventional identification relies largely on post-test standardized scores, which rarely reveal specific misconceptions, maladaptive behaviors such as wheel-spinning, or inefficient problem-solving strategies, delaying intervention. This systematic review, conducted in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, synthesizes research on explainable machine learning methods that use multimodal educational data, including interaction histories, clickstream data, eye-tracking, audiovisual classroom sensing, physiological cues, and contextual information, for the early detection and transparent explanation of mathematics learning difficulties. A March 2026 search of major databases and conference proceedings identified 18 sources. Interaction-log and clickstream data dominate early-warning systems, with decision-tree and gradient-boosting models commonly used to detect wheel-spinning, whereas eye-tracking provides process-level evidence of misconceptions and strategy use. Multimodal fusion approaches (early, late, hybrid/intermediate, and co-learning) combined with explainability methods (intrinsic glass-box models, Shapley additive explanations, local interpretable model-agnostic explanations, and counterfactual explanations) substantially improve predictive performance and interpretability, supporting educator trust and ethical deployment. Persistent challenges include reliance on proxy labels rather than clinical diagnoses, data alignment and synchronization, temporal and group leakage, limited cross-platform generalizability, and fairness. We propose a research agenda centered on privacy-preserving multimodal datasets, standardized evaluation of explanation usefulness for stakeholders, and integration with classroom interventions, and we discuss implications of the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act and U.S. and European data-protection laws.

items.title: The United States CADASIL Consortium: Baseline Findings from a Natural History Study
items.abstract_or_text: Background: and Objectives: Vascular contributions to cognitive impairment and dementia (VCID) represent the second leading cause of dementia and a common comorbidity for reduced functional capacity in many individuals, but clinical management and clinical trial readiness are severely hindered by extreme phenotypic and mechanistic heterogeneity. This study establishes the baseline clinical, functional, and multimodal biomarker characteristics of the first United States (US) cohort of Cerebral Autosomal Dominant Arteriopathy with Subcortical Infarcts and Leukoencephalopathy (CADASIL), serving as a single-cause, monogenic small vessel disease model for sporadic VCID. Methods: Cross-sectional analysis of baseline data collected from October 2022 through January 2025 from a longitudinal cohort at 12 US enrollment sites. Adults from families with a documented NOTCH3 variant were recruited through clinical referrals, medical record review, advocacy organizations, and community outreach. Exclusion criteria included other conditions that prevented interpretation of findings and modified Rankin Scale (mRS) scores greater than 3. Central genetic characterization assigned persons with a pathogenic or likely pathogenic NOTCH3 variant to low-, medium-, or high-risk tiers based on epidermal growth factor-like repeat domains. Standardized assessments included clinical histories, exams, objective cognitive and physical assessments, self-reported, companion-reported, and clinician-rated measures, MRI, genetics, and proteomics acquired under harmonized protocols. Group comparisons used Fishers exact and Kruskal-Wallis tests. Multivariable regression used adjustment for age, sex, race, and education. Results: Of 560 participants completing baseline visits, 46 had variants of unknown significance, and 55 had pending genetic analyses. The analytic cohort included 343 persons with a CADASIL-causing NOTCH3 variant and 116 non-carrier family controls. Median age was 47.9 years (IQR 38.7-59.1), median education was 16 years (IQR 14-17), 62.5% were female, and 91.4% were White. Carriers were classified in CADASIL risk tiers: low (7.0%), medium (18.4%), or high (74.6%). Compared with controls, adjusted odds of classification into a more impaired CDR category were higher in all tiers (OR 2.55-5.08, 95% CI 1.22-11.34). Discussion: The US CADASIL Consortium has established a large, genetics-confirmed cohort spanning presymptomatic to moderate disease stages, providing a robust, harmonized platform to define early biomarker signatures and endpoints for targeted VCID therapies.

items.title: Penicillin-clavulanate susceptibility in clinical methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus bloodstream infection strains from the CAMERA2 trial
items.abstract_or_text: Objectives: - Among clinical methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) bloodstream infection (BSI) strains, we sought to determine the prevalence of β-lactam-β-lactamase inhibitor (BLBLI) susceptibility, and its association with oxacillin susceptibility, genotypic factors, and patient characteristics. Methods- Clinical MRSA BSI strains were tested for susceptibility to penicillin-clavulanate by Etest (n=117, 36% of the dataset) and to oxacillin by disk diffusion assay (n=328, 100%). Penicillin-clavulanate susceptibility was defined as MIC ≤2mg/L and oxacillin disk susceptibility as an inhibition zone > 6mm. All strains were whole-genome sequenced, and alleles of mecA annotated. The sensitivity and specificity of the oxacillin disk to predict penicillin-clavulanate 'susceptibility' were assessed. Clinical and genomic associations with BLBLI 'susceptibility' were assessed by calculating odds-ratios (OR). Results -We found 73/117 (62%) and 205/328 (62%) strains to be 'susceptible' to penicillin-clavulanate and oxacillin disk, respectively. Oxacillin disk susceptibility and penicillin-clavulanate susceptibility were highly correlated (sensitivity 97.3% and specificity 95.5%). We therefore used oxacillin disk susceptibility as a proxy for penicillin-clavulanate susceptibility. Comparative genomics of the mecA gene uncovered 8 alleles. The oxacillin disk 'susceptible' phenotype was associated with specific mecA alleles, community-associated MRSA sequence-types (OR 72.8, 95%CI 35.4-162), community acquisition of infection (OR 2.09, 95% CI 1.03-4.27), lower Charlson Comorbidity Index (OR 0.90, 95% CI 0.82-0.98) and SOFA (sequential organ failure assessment) scores at presentation (OR 0.88, 95% CI 0.79-0.98). Conclusion - BLBLI 'susceptibility' is common among MRSA strains and is strongly associated with the strain genotype. Infections caused by BLBLI 'susceptible' strains are associated with specific patients' characteristics, namely younger age, fewer comorbidities, acquisition in the community and milder presentations.

items.title: Active machine learning using MCMC Bayesian neural networks
items.abstract_or_text: Background: Standard neural networks require large labelled datasets for strong generalization, which is often costly to annotate. Active learning (AL) reduces annotation costs by selecting the most informative samples for labelling based on model uncertainty, and Bayesian methods are a natural source of such uncertainty estimates. Approximate Bayesian methods such as Monte Carlo Dropout (MC Dropout) are scalable but can introduce systematic approximation errors in low-data regimes, whereas Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) provides higher-fidelity posterior estimates but is typically too computationally expensive for deep learning. We note that MCMC and AL are potentially complementary, since AL is designed to keep the labelled set small, which is exactly the regime in which MCMC is most tractable. Methods We investigate whether a small Bayesian neural network trained with MCMC outperforms a larger network using MC Dropout, when both use the same query function, Power Bayesian Active Learning by Disagreement (PowerBALD), across eight tabular classification datasets, an active learning setting with a 100-sample annotation budget, and matched supervised-learning baselines at 100 samples and at full training-set size. Results Within the 100-sample annotation budget, the small MCMC-based model achieved higher balanced accuracy than the MC Dropout model in 6 of 8 active learning tasks, and in 4 of 8 tasks in the matched 100-sample supervised setting, with one additional tie. The active learning procedure also matched or exceeded the performance of training on the full dataset in 5 of 8 tasks while using only a small fraction of the annotations. Conclusions These results suggest that MCMC is a viable and, in this constrained-budget setting, often preferable alternative to approximate Bayesian inference for active learning, though we do not claim that it is a generally superior inference method outside this low-annotation regime.

items.title: A Fractional Cyber–Biological Model for Energy-Aware Trust-Based Mobile-Agent Wireless Sensor Networks: Secure Plant-Disease Surveillance
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Low-power wireless sensor networks increasingly act as the measurement layer of biological decision systems, so a communication-security failure can propagate beyond the network and distort downstream biological inference. We formulate this interaction in two coupled layers. The cyber layer is a three-state Caputo fractional differential system for normalized residual energy, trust, and compromise probability under bounded selective-forwarding or on–off attack evidence. A mobile-agent utility rule converts these states into an energy-aware routing decision. items.title: Identification and Antimicrobial Susceptibility Profile of Bacterial Contaminants Isolated From Biofertilizer Bioreactors
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Microbial contamination in biofertilizer bioreactors represents a major challenge for industrial production, yet studies integrating molecular, phenotypic and antimicrobial characterization of bacterial contaminants remain limited. Bacterial isolates recovered from biofertilizer bioreactors with process deviations were identified by 16S rRNA gene sequencing (primers 27F/1492R) and further characterized by phenotypic and biochemical assays. Antimicrobial susceptibility was determined by the Kirby–Bauer disk diffusion method, while the antibacterial activity of a hydroethanolic extract of Copaifera malmei was evaluated by broth microdilution and membrane permeability assays. The isolates were identified as Micrococcus luteus and Bacillus cereus sensu lato, showing > 99% 16S rRNA gene sequence similarity. The B. cereus isolate exhibited multidrug resistance to ampicillin, penicillin, cefoxitin and ceftazidime, remaining susceptible only to tetracycline and erythromycin. Phenotypic and biochemical analyses corroborated the molecular identification of the B. cereus isolate. In contrast, M. luteus was susceptible to all antimicrobials tested. The hydroethanolic extract of C. malmei showed limited antibacterial activity, with minimum inhibitory concentrations of 5000 µg/mL against B. cereus and 312 µg/mL against M. luteus , although membrane permeability assays indicated increased leakage of intracellular material in the latter. The integration of molecular, phenotypic and antimicrobial susceptibility analyses provides a robust approach for the characterization of bacterial contaminants in biofertilizer bioreactors. The multidrug-resistant profile of the B. cereus isolate reinforces the importance of continuous microbiological surveillance and stricter sanitation strategies in industrial biofertilizer production.

items.title: Responsible AI Governance for Vaccine Safety and Pharmacovigilance in Nigeria: A Policy Review of Risks, Regulatory Gaps, and Implementation Pathways
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Nigeria’s expanding immunization programs and increasing availability of real-world health data create an urgent need to strengthen vaccine safety surveillance and pharmacovigilance. Artificial intelligence (AI) can improve adverse event detection, signal management, and risk communication by processing large, complex, and rapidly generated datasets. However, deploying AI in high-stakes public health systems also creates policy and governance risks, including data privacy vulnerabilities, algorithmic bias, opacity in decision-making, and unclear liability. This paper examines how responsible AI can be governed within Nigeria’s vaccine safety and pharmacovigilance systems. We synthesize peer-reviewed grey literature published between 2016 and 2026, international and continental governance instruments, including WHO guidance on AI for health, the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, the European Union AI Act, and the African Union Continental AI Strategy. We also analyze relevant Nigerian institutions and instruments, including NAFDAC, NPHCDA, the Nigeria Data Protection Act (2023), and the emerging national AI policy environment. Five priority governance challenges are identified: data privacy and security; algorithmic bias and equity; transparency and explainability; accountability across institutions; and public trust amid vaccine misinformation. Regulatory instruments provide important foundations but are not sufficient for AI-enabled pharmacovigilance without sector-specific operational guidance. The paper proposes a phased, multistakeholder governance framework incorporating an AI Steering Group, risk-based classification of AI tools, strengthened data stewardship, regulatory sandbox implementation, and measurable performance indicators.

items.title: Muscle fibre-resolved spatial transcriptomics of regeneration, necrosis and border zones in human paraspinal muscle
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Focal necrotizing lesion fields in human skeletal muscle contain a mosaic of necrotic fibres, regenerative fibres, and morphologically preserved neighbouring fibres, but their fibre-resolved molecular organisation remains poorly defined. We applied targeted Xenium spatial transcriptomics to a human lumbar paraspinal muscle biopsy with toxic myopathy and integrated the analysis with serial post-run hematoxylin and eosin stain, adult and neonatal myosin heavy-chain isoforms, immunostaining for membrane attack complex of complement (C5b9) and manual fibre-level region-of-interest segmentation. Distant normal type 1 and type 2 fibres, necrotic fibres, regenerative fibres, and intact type 1 and type 2 fibres immediately adjacent to necrosis or regeneration were compared. Baseline transcriptional differences between distant normal type 1 and type 2 fibres were modest, whereas lesion-associated contrasts were substantially broader, indicating that pathological state outweighed basal fibre identity within this targeted panel. Necrotic fibre regions were enriched for immune/myeloid-associated transcripts, including PLA2G7 , TREM2 , FCGR3A , MS4A4A , CD163 , MRC1 , and PTPRC , whereas regenerative fibres preferentially expressed structural and calcium-handling genes, including MYBPC1 , DES , MEF2C , S100A1 , and PVALB . Despite preserved morphology, fibres bordering necrosis displayed a pronounced border-zone signature that largely overlapped the necrotic programme, whereas neighbourhood effects around regeneration were weaker and fibre-type dependent. These findings define necrosis, regeneration, and their border zones as distinct spatial states within a focal human muscle lesion and indicate that fibres adjacent to necrosis, despite being morphologically normal, are unsuitable internal comparators.

items.title: Pretraining Beyond Birds: Multi-Taxa Acoustic Representation Learning for Pantanal Biodiversity Monitoring
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Passive acoustic monitoring enables scalable biodiversity assessment, yet automated species identification remains challenging in multi-taxa ecosystems. We present a deep learning pipeline for BirdCLEF 2026, targeting 234 species across five taxonomic classes in the Pantanal wetland of Brazil, achieving AUROC 0.960 (public) and 0.959 (private), ranking 19th selected and 3rd unselected. Three key contributions emerge from 288 systematic experiments. First, multi-taxa backbone pretraining on 9,257 species including Amphibia, Insecta, Mammalia, and Reptilia yields +0.016 AUROC over bird-only pretraining — critical as 31% of target species are non-bird. Second, we identify a calibration-quality paradox in pseudo-label generation: a better-calibrated teacher model (AUROC 0.946) produces lower-quality pseudo labels than a weaker teacher (AUROC 0.930), degrading performance by 0.032 AUROC. Third, taxonomic smoothing — blending predictions with genus and class means — provides a zero-cost +0.001 AUROC gain. Our findings offer practical guidance for multi-taxa bioacoustic monitoring in conservation applications.

items.title: Plasticity degeneracy underlies flexible formation and reconfiguration of spatial representations in hippocampal granule cells
items.abstract_or_text: Learning and memory require neural representations that are simultaneously robust and adaptable. How do neural systems reconcile these opposing demands of stability and flexibility? Here, we use hippocampal granule cells, which transform spatially diffuse entorhinal inputs into sparse sharply-tuned spatial representations, to address this fundamental question using emergence, stabilization, remapping, and suppression of place-fields as ideal systems to study stability-flexibility balance. Employing an unbiased population-based approach involving different strengths of plasticity in several components, we show that sharply tuned place-cell firing does not arise from a unique plasticity mechanism. We employed a population of heterogeneous, experimentally constrained biophysical models of dentate gyrus granule cells receiving cortical grid-field and contextual inputs to demonstrate that spatially restricted synaptic potentiation is insufficient to selectively route spatial information. Instead, each of the four distinct target transitions, namely reliable emergence, stabilization, remapping, and suppression of place-fields, were achievable by coordinated plasticity spanning excitatory synapses and several intrinsic ion channels. Across each of these four transitions, we identify numerous mechanistically distinct plasticity combinations that generate equivalent functional outcomes. These solutions are non-random and highly diverse, exhibiting weak dependence among individual plasticity components despite converging onto constrained functional states, through a combination of targeted amplification and global suppression of spatial firing. Our findings reveal extensive plasticity degeneracy in hippocampal spatial coding and suggest that flexible neural representations emerge not from unique plasticity rules involving one single component, but from a repertoire of alternative plasticity routes that are capable of implementing the same computation.

items.title: Depth-wise super-resolution of a serial-sectioned low-carbon steel microstructure by a generative adversarial network trained on in-plane images
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract In this study, a deep-learning super-resolution framework that restores the depth-wise resolution of the 3D microstructure of a low-carbon steel without the need of additional training data is presented. The 3D microstructure of a metallic material is generally obtained through serial sectioning followed by observation of the sample surface. This provides a full 3D image, but its resolution along the depth direction is low compared to that of the microscope-observed planes. Various deep learning methods have been developed to overcome this limitation, but they mostly require additional 3D microstructure datasets to train the networks. Here, an enhanced super-resolution generative adversarial network (ESRGAN) trained on low and high resolution pairs was employed to restore the depth-wise resolution of the microstructure. As the pairs were generated internally from the specimen's own surface images, the trained network was applied along the depth direction without any external dataset. Together with a conventional SRGAN, a super-resolution convolutional neural network (SRCNN) and three interpolation schemes, we compared the methods in terms of microstructural and statistical analysis, as well as structural similarity. Among the compared methods, the ESRGAN provided the most faithful reconstruction of the depth-wise microstructure.

items.title: Prospective evaluation of a deep learning model for classifying pediatric septal defects on grayscale echocardiographic videos: comparison with three pediatric cardiologists
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Background Timely recognition of atrial and ventricular septal defects (ASDs and VSDs) remains challenging in settings where access to pediatric echocardiography expertise is limited. We prospectively evaluated a locked deep learning model for standalone classification of pediatric grayscale echocardiographic videos and compared its performance with that of three pediatric cardiologists under the same grayscale-only test condition. Methods Patients younger than 18 years undergoing clinically indicated transthoracic echocardiography at a tertiary pediatric cardiac center were screened prospectively. Participants were enrolled consecutively within each reference-standard diagnostic stratum until 35 were included in each class: ASD, VSD, and normal heart. The locked model and three blinded pediatric cardiologists independently classified identical de-identified grayscale videos without Doppler or clinical information. A single consultant pediatric cardiologist established the reference-standard diagnosis from the complete clinical echocardiographic examination. items.title: The hydrocup: a hollow electrospun scaffold for in vivo hydrogel-laden cell delivery
items.abstract_or_text: For regenerative medicine applications, transplanted cells are difficult to retain in a specific place to maximize the localized release of cytokines, which can positively modulate immune responses, angiogenesis and tissue regeneration. Here, we developed a hollow electrospun (ESP) scaffold with one open and one closed end to enclose a hydrogel laden with human mesenchymal stem cells (hMSCs); we termed this combination the hydrocup. hMSCs remained viable for 28 days in vitro and released functional cytokines similar to hMSCs in transplanted but non-enclosed hydrogels. The hydrocups remained intact and fixed in place for 6 weeks after subcutaneous implantation in rats, demonstrating in vivo compatibility. These results demonstrate that the hydrocup is the first, to our knowledge, cell-laden hydrogel delivery scaffold. This innovation could be developed for a wide variety of cell-based cytokine secretion or drug-laden hydrogel applications.

items.title: Which disadvantaged students beat the odds in STEM? A design-consistent, fairness-audited machine learning study of 143,573 adolescents in 79 PISA 2022 education systems
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Socio-economically disadvantaged students who nonetheless reach solid proficiency in mathematics and science (“STEM-resilient” students) show that disadvantage does not preclude STEM success, and identifying the factors that accompany such resilience is a policy priority. Machine learning studies of international large-scale assessment data have begun to address related questions, but existing work pools students without respecting the assessments’ complex survey design, evaluates models only on in-distribution splits, applies a single outcome definition, and has not yet examined whether models err evenly across student groups. Guided by an ecological, contextually situated account of academic resilience, this study used PISA 2022 data from 143,573 disadvantaged adolescents (weighted bottom socio-economic quartile within each of 79 systems) to predict STEM resilience, defined as proficiency Level 3 or above in both mathematics and science, treating all ten plausible values as multiple imputations, weighting estimation and evaluation, and grouping cross-validation by school. STEM resilience characterized 12.5% of disadvantaged students internationally (population-weighted; SE = 0.3%), with system rates ranging from below 0.1% to 62%. A gradient-boosting model predicted resilience accurately and with excellent calibration (AUC = 0.912; 95% cluster-bootstrap CI 0.909–0.914; PR-AUC = 0.688; slope = 0.996), against 0.862 for logistic regression and 0.801 for a system-base-rate-only baseline. Mathematics self-efficacy was the strongest predictor, and rankings were nearly invariant across plausible values (τ = .90). Models transported imperfectly to unseen systems (median held-out AUC = 0.847), and system-specific factor hierarchies diverged from the pooled hierarchy (median τ = .30) beyond a sampling-noise benchmark (τ = .45), although self-efficacy ranked first under every outcome definition. At a prevalence-matched threshold, the model detected resilient girls (59.4% vs 65.6%) and rural students (53.9% vs 66.1%) less often than their counterparts; an attribute-blind refit removed the gender gap but not the rural gap. Ignoring weights or clustering changed results little; changing the outcome definition changed them most. Protective factors associated with STEM resilience are only partly universal, and single-threshold screening uses would overlook resilient girls and rural students. The study offers a design-consistent, transport-tested, fairness-audited template for machine learning with international assessment data.

items.title: Does Deep Learning Vascular Segmentation on CTA Improve Vertebral Artery Dissection Detection?
items.abstract_or_text: Purpose: The aims of this study were to develop an externally validated deep learning vascular segmentation model for digital enhancement of vertebral artery dissection detection on CTA and to assess clinical utility of the model through a paired crossover reader study. Materials and Methods: This retrospective, IRB-approved study conducted from September 2024 to July 2026 included an internal training cohort of 84 manually segmented CTAs plus 17 CTAs from the RSNA Intracranial Aneurysm Challenge (101 CTAs total) and an external testing cohort of 40 CTAs (22 positive, 18 negative for vertebral artery dissection). A nnU-Net (version 2) model was trained using five-fold cross-validation with the entire training cohort. Technical performance was evaluated using the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC). items.title: Development and Internal Validation of a Machine-Learning Model to Identify Low Clinical Teaching Self-Efficacy Among Nurse Preceptors: A Multicenter Cross-Sectional Study
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Background: Clinical teaching self-efficacy influences nurse preceptors’ teaching engagement and practice, yet routinely collected professional and teaching-related information may not adequately identify preceptors who need additional support. We aimed to develop and internally evaluate a model for identifying low clinical teaching self-efficacy among nurse preceptors. Methods: This multicenter cross-sectional study included 1,221 nurse preceptors from four hospitals in Guangyuan, Sichuan Province, China, between February and June 2026. Candidate predictors were conceptually organized according to social cognitive theory. Low clinical teaching self-efficacy was operationally defined using the 25th percentile of the total score. Predictors were selected using bias-reduced logistic regression. The sample was split 75:25 into training and test sets. Logistic regression and seven machine-learning models were compared using discrimination, calibration, Brier score, decision-curve analysis, and Shapley additive explanations (SHAP). Results: Among 1,221 preceptors, 322 were classified as having low clinical teaching self-efficacy. Five predictors were retained: total Tacit Knowledge Sharing Scale (TKSS) score, frequency of participation in clinical teaching-related training, years of clinical teaching experience, years of nursing experience, and organizational position. In the test set, the neural network and Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) achieved areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUCs) of 0.936 and 0.934, respectively, with no statistically significant difference. LightGBM had a sensitivity of 0.840, specificity of 0.822, positive predictive value of 0.630, negative predictive value of 0.934, and Brier score of 0.083; its calibration intercept was −0.163 and calibration slope was 0.989. LightGBM was among the models with the highest net benefit across threshold probabilities of approximately 5%–60%. Given its overall performance across discrimination, calibration, prediction error, and decision-curve analysis, LightGBM was selected for model interpretation. SHAP analysis ranked tacit knowledge sharing as the most influential predictor. Conclusions: In the held-out test set, LightGBM showed a favorable balance of discrimination, calibration, prediction error, and decision-curve net benefit. If externally validated, the model could help identify preceptors who may benefit from further assessment and targeted preceptor-development support.

Multimodal Sensitivity Enhancement of Binding-based Diagnostic Assays Using Functional Hydrogels
items.abstract_or_text: Immunoassays are critical for clinical diagnostics, yet their performance is restricted by the physical constraints of flat surfaces used to immobilize capture molecules which limit loading capacity and induce protein denaturation. Hydrogels provide immense volumetric molecular loading capacity but translating them across diverse assay formats and readout modalities without compromising analyte permeability remains challenging. Here, we present a universal strategy for hydrogel integration into immunoassay platforms for enhanced optical and electronic biosensing. Utilizing bio-orthogonal photo-click chemistry, we developed a modular and tuneable poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) matrix that achieves a 6,000-fold increase in molecular loading and a large mesh size for analyte diffusion. This 3D architecture demonstrates broad multimodal utility with easy integration into a range of binding-based assays enabling higher sensitivity, repeatability and multiplexability. It achieves high sensitivity enhancement for fluorescence detection in microarrays (38-fold) and microtiter plates (25-fold) and enables multiplexed readout in single wells, including from clinical serum samples. In silver metallization-based assays it boosts densitometric optical detection sensitivity (18-fold) and enables inexpensive electronic detection. In lateral flow assays, it generates 20-fold signal enhancement while enabling multiplexability and higher repeatability. By standardizing high-capacity volumetric biosensing, this scalable, plug-and-play technology empowers next generation highly sensitive, field-deployable point-of-care diagnostics.

items.title: Disruption of lamina-associated genome organization activates neuronal gene programs in H3.3K27M DIPG
items.abstract_or_text: Diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma (DIPG) is a fatal pediatric brain tumor frequently driven by a histone H3 mutation that substitutes lysine 27 with methionine (H3K27M). While H3K27M is known to cause a global depletion of the repressive histone mark H3K27me3, how this epigenetic disruption contributes to oncogenic transcriptional reprogramming remains incompletely understood. Here, we show that H3.3K27M DIPG cells exhibit widespread disruption of lamina-associated domain (LAD) organization across primary tumors and patient-derived cell lines. H3.3K27M was enriched at genomic regions that lost lamina association, which acquired increased H3K27ac and showed activation of neuronal and oncogenic gene programs. Notably, LAD loss was more strongly associated with transcriptional activation than H3K27me3 depletion, linking altered LAD organization to the transcriptional consequences of H3.3K27M. Finally, expression of H3.3K27M in human embryonic stem cell-derived neural precursor cells (NPCs) was sufficient to induce LAD remodeling, predominantly through loss of lamina association, leading to activation of neuronal gene programs. Together, these findings identify disruption of lamina-associated genome architecture as a key mechanism by which the H3.3K27M oncohistone drives oncogenic transcriptional reprogramming in DIPG.

items.title: From Genes to Brains: Molecular Evolution and Mammalian Brain Cellular Diversity
items.abstract_or_text: Mammalian brains exhibit extensive diversity in size, cellular composition, and organization, yet the molecular evolutionary changes associated with this phenotypic diversification remain incompletely understood. Here, we investigated whether protein-sequence evolution covaries with quantitative differences in brain phenotypes across mammals. We integrated 29 brain and body traits with orthologous protein sequences from 18 mammalian species and obtained gene-specific molecular evolutionary measures for 10,395 genes. To reduce redundancy among strongly correlated phenotypes, we selected five representative traits that explained 88.12% of the standardized trait variance under linear reconstruction. Using RERconverge, we tested for associations between gene-specific relative evolutionary rates and evolutionary changes in these five representative traits. The primary analysis, based on log-transformed phenotypes, identified 25 significant gene--trait associations involving 23 genes, 19 of which were also recovered using untransformed phenotypes, indicating that a substantial subset of the associations was robust to phenotype transformation. Expression profiling of these shared candidate genes across adult human GTEx brain tissues revealed heterogeneous patterns ranging from broad expression across the examined tissues to low adult brain expression. Functional enrichment analysis further showed that the gene set retained for comparative analysis was enriched for diverse biological processes, including metabolic, cellular, and neural pathways. These results identify gene-specific evolutionary-rate associations with quantitative mammalian phenotypes and provide functional context for the genes represented in the comparative analysis. Our study provides a comparative framework linking relative evolutionary rates of protein-coding genes to quantitative variation in mammalian brain cellular architecture while accounting for shared evolutionary history.

items.title: AutoWrinkleID: a machine learning pipeline for biofilm wrinkle identification and quantitative analysis
items.abstract_or_text: Biofilms are widely distributed in both natural and engineered systems and play a fundamental role in microbial ecology and biotechnological applications. When grown on agar substrates, biofilms often exhibit macroscopic structural features due to mechanical instabilities driven by matrix production. These wrinkles encode relevant information about biofilm growth and structural development and have even been shown to possess some functional roles. Despite their relevance, currently available approaches for wrinkle detection from images rely on manual annotation, which is time-consuming, not scalable, and strongly dependent on the annotator. In the present study, we developed an end-to-end machine learning pipeline, named AutoWrinkleID, that starts from bright field images of biofilms and performs wrinkle identification, characterisation, and quantification across multiple bacterial species and strains. The name reflects the automated identification and subsequent characterisation and quantification of biofilm wrinkles. The annotations used to generate the masks, namely images containing only the wrinkle structures, were obtained both through manual labelling and using constitutive fluorescence and motility fluorescence. Interestingly, we found that models trained using only manual annotations perform worse than those trained using motility fluorescence markers. A comparison between motility and constitutive fluorescence masks further indicates that motility based annotations consistently outperform constitutive fluorescence across all strains, strongly suggesting that motile phenotypes are tightly associated with wrinkle structures. Additional computational analysis is conducted on the same dataset to assess the robustness and limitations of the results as a function of training dataset. We also observed that Sholl analysis, originally developed for the study of neuronal dendrites and later applied to wrinkle analysis, can effectively characterize wrinkle patterns, although its applicability is strongly limited by wrinkle shape and by the quality of the masks.

items.title: SafeAgent-300: A Balanced 300-Prompt Benchmark for Agentic AI Security, with Findings on Detector Coverage Gaps and Cross-Model Compliance Variance
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract We present SafeAgent-300, a balanced adversarial prompt benchmark foragentic AI security spanning ten categories under an author-designed,OWASP-inspired taxonomy (see Sect. 4 forthe exact relationship to OWASP's own published documents, to which wedo not claim direct correspondence), with exactly 30 prompts percategory and 10 per (category, difficulty-tier) cell across threetiers. We collected responses from all 300 prompts against a six-modelroster, producing 1{,}800 labeled trials, scored under a pattern-baseddetector suite hardened over the course of this work. We report threefindings: a previously-unreported spontaneous tool-invocation behaviorin one Google Gemini model; a substantial, independently-corroboratedspread in model conservatism across the roster; and an apparentinverse relationship between prompt sophistication and detectedviolation rate that we partially retract on further investigation,substantially -- though not entirely -- an artifact of uneven detectorcoverage. We document the coverage gap, the fixes applied to three offive affected detectors, and the work required to close the remainingtwo. We release the prompt library as open-source software; raw modelcompletions are withheld since some contain functional exploittechnique, with de-identified aggregate data and defanged examplesavailable in the paper, and full raw data available on request under adata-use agreement.

items.title: Protecting the Learner in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: An Educational Psychology Policy Agenda for Student Well-Being, Agency and Resilience in Sub-Saharan Africa
items.abstract_or_text: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly changing education through generative AI, adaptive learning systems, automated assessment, intelligent teaching, and data-driven learning support. More and more AI-powered systems are mediating learning, communication, information searching, and, in some cases, emotional support. These technologies offer great promise for enhancing access, personalization, efficiency, and learner engagement, but they also present substantial psychological, ethical, and developmental problems. These challenges are exacerbated in Sub-Saharan Africa by inequalities in digital access, inadequate regulatory capacity, insufficient data-protection systems, language and cultural under-representation, and uneven institutional preparation. Policy and implications In this policy brief, we look at AI in education from the perspective of educational psychology, with a special emphasis on student well-being, learner agency, and resilience. It proposes that AI governance should extend beyond considerations of technology adoption and academic efficiency to explore how AI impacts autonomy, motivation, critical thinking, creativity, social relationships, psychological safety, and autonomous learning. The report emphasizes the importance of learner-centered national AI policies, age-appropriate safeguards, increased teacher capacity, inclusion of AI literacy in curricula, safeguarding of learner data, equal access to digital technology, culturally relevant artificial intelligence systems, and meaningful student participation in AI governance. Policies should ensure that AI is used to promote learning, yet safeguard student well-being, autonomy, privacy, dignity, and cognitive growth. It also underscores the need for African-led research and cross-sector collaboration to generate context-specific information on the long-term implications of AI for learners. Recommendations The brief argues that the success of AI integration in Sub-Saharan African education should be gauged not just by the acceptance of technology, but by its contribution to psychologically healthy, critically thinking, resilient, and autonomous learners. Conclusions A human-centered approach is therefore very important to ensuring that AI is a help and not a hindrance to the developmental and relational underpinnings of education.

items.title: Stage-resolved analysis of posterior regeneration in Ophryotrocha labronica reveals early pluripotency activation and conserved regenerative programs
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Background Regeneration is a widespread post-embryonic process across metazoans and particularly diverse among annelids, offering a valuable system to explore how complex tissues are restored and why regenerative capacity varies across species. While morphological aspects of regeneration, including nervous system reconstruction, have been extensively described, the underlying cellular and molecular mechanisms remain poorly resolved in many non-model annelids, particularly at stage-specific resolution. Results Here, we characterise posterior regeneration in the dorvilleid annelid Ophryotrocha labronica by integrating morphological, cellular, neuroanatomical, and transcriptomic approaches. We define a temporal framework from wound healing to complete tail regeneration within five days, focusing on mid-early proliferative and differentiation stages. Proliferation and stem cell-related genes contribute to blastema formation and early differentiation, while neurogenesis-related genes activate shortly after injury and persist throughout regeneration, suggesting a sustained role in coordinating blastema development. This process involves both local and migratory proliferative cells, preceded by early activation of pluripotency and neural markers. Comparative analyses further reveal both conserved and lineage-specific mechanisms in O. labronica , highlighting shared molecular pathways as well as evolutionary divergence across annelids. Conclusions Our results provide stage-resolved insights into the molecular regulation of posterior regeneration in O. labronica . Conserved signalling pathways (Notch, Hedgehog, Wnt) alongside candidates such as NOX2/CYBB, previously described in vertebrate regeneration, highlight shared and lineage-specific mechanisms underlying regenerative diversity. These findings underscore the value of non-model annelids for understanding the evolution and diversity of regenerative strategies across metazoans.
